Game on the sports feed this cycle: Oaks at KONO — One game after their first home loss, the Oaks beat Denver 137-113 at home in a non-Cup game in front of a 94 percent crowd. The city is buying in. Oakland led 38-36 after one, 71-59 at the half and 103-79 after three, and played the Nuggets even in the fourth, 34-34. Austin Reaves led the Oaks with 32 points in just 22 minutes, 8 of 14 from the field, 6 of 10 from three and 10 of 10 at the line, with 4 rebounds, 3 assists, a steal and no turnovers. That makes 27 and 32 in his two games against Denver this season. T. Jerome kept his run going off the bench with a 14-point, 11-assist double-double in 25 minutes on 5 of 8 shooting and 4 of 5 from three. He has scored in double figures four straight games: 19, 28, 23 and 14. Wendell Carter Jr. had 17 points and 6 rebounds on 6 of 9, his third straight game in double figures after 17 and 14, and AJ Dybantsa added 15 on 7 of 11 after 18 and 19 in his last two. As a team the Oaks shot 48 of 92, 52 percent, and 21 of 43 from three, 49 percent, with 31 assists, though they turned it over 22 times. The Oaks move to 10-2 and remain 2-1 in Cup play. (the rider lift is real only where a station row says "game day")

Game on the sports feed this cycle: Oaks at San Antonio — The Oaks went on the road to face the Golden State Warriors, the team that used to call Oakland home and left, and beat them 98-96 in a Cup game. The last time these teams met it went the other way. In C109 the Warriors came to Oakland for game 2 of the preseason and beat the Oaks, one of the nine straight losses the Oaks took through rookie camp and the preseason. The first meeting that counted went to Oakland, on the Warriors' floor. Oakland trailed 25-14 after one and 59-44 at the half, down 15. The Oaks cut it to 78-74 after a 30-19 third quarter and won the fourth 24-18, outscoring Golden State 54-37 in the second half. Austin Reaves led the Oaks again with 23 points, 6 rebounds, 5 assists and 3 steals in 33 minutes on 9 of 17 shooting and 3 of 6 from three. T. Jerome scored 17 in 23 minutes on 7 of 13 and 3 of 8 from three with no turnovers, his fifth straight game in double figures: 19, 28, 23, 14 and 17. AJ Dybantsa added 12, getting to the line for 5 of 7, his fourth straight game in double figures after 18, 19 and 15. As a team the Oaks shot 39 of 88, 44 percent, and 9 of 34 from three, with 23 assists and 23 turnovers, and won it in the second half. The Oaks move to 11-2 and 3-1 in Cup play. (the rider lift is real only where a station row says "game day")

sources.name: Eleanor Rivera
sources.quote: Game days at 12th are a different animal — you can feel it before you even see the platform. The crowd comes in waves, not a steady stream, and that's what stretches the dwell time. Trains are there on time, but everyone's squeezing on at once, so the doors hold longer and the schedule slips a little. My crew just adjusts — no big announcements, everyone knows their spot. We read the rhythm of the station, and we move with it. It's not glamorous, but when the platforms fill up like that, you see the team do what they do best: keep it moving, keep it safe, keep it human.

sources.name: Elena Soria Dominguez
sources.quote: Look, I'll be straight with you — the visioning phase isn't what's moving riders on the platform. People aren't staring at renderings on their way to work. Fruitvale's down this cycle, and I can tell you the design process doesn't put a single butt on a seat. What it does is make sure that when we do break ground, the station actually works for the people who live here — the cart vendors, the kids walking to BART, the folks transferring at rush hour. The ridership numbers right now track with what's happening in East Oakland — events, crowds, the energy of the neighborhood. The hub is about what Fruitvale looks like in five years, not what the counter says this week. I don't pretend otherwise.

sources.name: Ximena Mehta
sources.quote: Honestly, the ridership jump at 12th doesn't surprise me one bit — between the Baylight construction finally moving and everything happening around the lake and Jack London, that station is the hub everyone funnels through. But yeah, the on-time piece is the part that keeps me up. When you've got that many people on the platforms and the line's running tight, every little delay compounds. The workers on the roster see it from the platform — it's not one big problem, it's the crowd itself slowing the doors, the dwell times stretching. I think the congestion factor is real, and it's the price of the city actually showing up. We just have to figure out how to move that many people without the schedule paying for it.

sources.name: Evan Lewis
sources.quote: I drive that corridor every day, and you can feel it. The platforms are packed, especially on game days and when something's happening at Lake Merritt or down in Jack London. But the trains aren't always there when they should be. We see it from the platform — the crowd's growing, but the schedule's slipping. It's not one thing; it's the construction, the events, the whole city moving at once. We're doing what we can, but the riders feel it, and so do we.

sources.name: Elena Soria Dominguez
sources.quote: Here's what's on the sheet, and what I can and can't tell you from it. 12th Street gained 1,962 riders this cycle and its on-time performance fell four points, 0.81 to 0.77. The Factors column is where the answer lives: 12th Street is carrying game-day crowds — Oaks home week, traffic through Jack London and Downtown — plus Baylight District construction, events in Lake Merritt and West Oakland, and crowded platforms across the system. When a platform is full and the streets feeding it are jammed, trains dwell longer. That's the mechanism, and it's the same one I described last cycle. I'm not going to invent a cause the sheet doesn't show, and there are no BART train events at 12th Street this cycle — the one event on the sheet is a clean run at Lake Merritt, no delay. Is it showing elsewhere? Partly, and not evenly. 19th Street actually improved, 0.78 to 0.81, despite its own game-day crowds. Lake Merritt went 0.77 to 0.84. West Oakland 0.79 to 0.86. MacArthur 0.78 to 0.85. So the slip is not a system-wide slide — it's concentrated at 12th Street, which is what you'd expect given it's the station taking the heaviest event traffic. My stations: Fruitvale is at 0.85, up from 0.83, with 8,007 riders. Coliseum is at 0.82. I'll be straight with you — Fruitvale's ridership is down from 9,343 last cycle. I said last week the numbers follow life, not a drawing, and I'll hold to that in both directions: I won't claim the gain as the hub's credit and I won't dress up the drop. Nothing has been built. Corridors: I-880 North is back to 100, heavy, with event traffic and the Baylight construction — the gridlock day put the traffic index at 83, worst on I-880 North. I-980 100, also event traffic. I-880 South 93, I-580 East 82, I-580 West 80, International Blvd 84 — International has gone back from moderate to heavy, and that's the corridor my neighbors walk and cross, so I'm watching it. Broadway 73 and Grand 65 are the only moderate ones. So yes, the corridors are showing the same pressure the 12th Street platform is. Bottom line: crowded platforms on event weeks plus construction-adjacent congestion is your on-time story at 12th Street. 19th Street ran better, most stations ran better. I don't have a cause in the record beyond that, and I won't manufacture one for you.

I said last week the numbers follow life, not a drawing, and I'll hold to that in both directions: I won't claim the gain as the hub's credit and I won't dress up the drop. Nothing has been built. Corridors: I-880 North is back to 100, heavy, with event traffic and the Baylight construction — the gridlock day put the traffic index at 83, worst on I-880 North. I-980 100, also event traffic. I-880 South 93, I-580 East 82, I-580 West 80, International Blvd 84 — International has gone back from moderate to heavy, and that's the corridor my neighbors walk and cross, so I'm watching it. Broadway 73 and Grand 65 are the only moderate ones. So yes, the corridors are showing the same pressure the 12th Street platform is. Bottom line: crowded platforms on event weeks plus construction-adjacent congestion is your on-time story at 12th Street. 19th Street ran better, most stations ran better. I don't have a cause in the record beyond that, and I won't manufacture one for you.
